headline: Milburn review calls for 'complete system reset' on education and welfare to get 440,000 young people into work
summary: Alan Milburn's major review of Britain's youth jobs crisis recommends sweeping reforms across education, work and welfare systems. The number of young people not in education, employment or training has surged to almost a million. Milburn, a former Tony Blair-era health secretary, is urging Andy Burnham to invest billions in a "new deal" for young people, including guaranteed jobs support funded partly by reducing benefits. The report frames this as a critical moment for policy, warning of a "downward escalator" trapping young people into welfare dependency. Around a third of young people who persistently skip school in Years 10 and 11 go on to become NEET, the government believes.

headline: Burnham signals Labour openness to reversing Brexit red lines after declaring the deal 'has not worked'
summary: Andy Burnham has told an audience at the Lord Mayor's Banquet that Brexit "has not worked" and that Britain lost more than it gained. Speaking ahead of an EU summit, the Prime Minister signalled that Labour could drop its longstanding red lines on Europe, saying he will begin new discussions with the EU about options for Britain's "long-term relationship" after the Brussels meeting. Burnham stated that Britain's global standing has been "dramatically diminished" in the decade since the 2016 referendum. Transport campaigners have separately urged him to invest in international rail services, specifically calling for reopened Eurostar stations in Kent and new infrastructure at London St Pancras, as a way to reset the UK-EU relationship.

headline: Vote Leave architects claim £750m weekly cost to rejoin EU, echoing contested Leave campaign bus figures
summary: Former Vote Leave campaigners have published analysis claiming that rejoining the EU would cost Britain £750 million per week. The Guardian's analysis questions the reliability of these figures, drawing a parallel to the contested £350m-per-week claim on the Leave campaign's bus during the 2016 referendum. The report notes that the Vote Leave figures are described as "very selective," suggesting they may misrepresent the actual economic costs and benefits of EU membership in a way analogous to disputed claims made during the original Brexit campaign.
bias_label: centre-left outlet questioning Leave campaign analysis

headline: Asylum seekers on final 'one-in-one-out' deportation flight report threats from smugglers, face immediate removal rules
summary: On Tuesday's final "one in, one out" UK-France deportation flight, many asylum seekers are being deported for a second time. Hundreds who were originally sent back to France have since returned to the UK citing threats from people smugglers who demanded further payment for the Channel crossing, saying families still owed money. Meanwhile, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is amending a bill to strip failed asylum applicants of a five-day grace period, allowing immigration enforcement to detain and remove people immediately after their appeals are exhausted. Refugee charities have condemned the removal of this grace period as distressing and unnecessary. The two-part policy—the ending of the "one in, one out" programme and the accelerated removal rules—represents a hardening of the government's asylum stance.

headline: US and allies coordinate to protect AI technology and infrastructure from China rivalry
summary: The United States and its allies are coordinating efforts to protect artificial intelligence technology and infrastructure amid growing strategic competition with China. The scope and specific measures of this coordination are not detailed in available sources, but the initiative reflects concern about China's technological advancement and the need for collective security measures among Western nations on critical AI development.

headline: China uses US AI models to train domestic competitors while facing semiconductor export restrictions
summary: According to a Reuters exclusive report, China is leveraging US-developed artificial intelligence models to train and develop its own competing systems, even as US-led chip export restrictions tighten. The practice represents a workaround to American curbs on semiconductor exports, which are intended to slow China's AI advancement. This highlights the difficulty of enforcing technological containment when open-source or publicly available models from US companies can be adapted and used to train Chinese alternatives.

headline: Miliband says he won't resign if government approves controversial Rosebank oil field
summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is making a decision on whether to approve development of Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil field. Ed Miliband, the Environment Secretary, has stated that he will not resign if the government gives the green light to the project, suggesting a split within the cabinet between ministers who favour development and those with environmental concerns. The decision over Rosebank is a test of the government's climate credentials and industrial policy balance.

headline: Five EU countries establish Rwanda migrant deportation hub, mirroring UK asylum policy model
summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have jointly announced plans to establish a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers in Rwanda. This move mirrors the approach previously pursued by the UK and reflects a broader European trend toward outsourcing asylum processing and deportations to third countries outside the EU. The coordination among five significant EU member states suggests growing support for such offshore processing arrangements, though the countries involved and their specific arrangements with Rwanda have not been detailed in available sources.

headline: UK Budget Introduces World-First Ring-Fence for Preventative Spending
summary: Chancellor John Healey's budget introduces a world-first policy: a preventative departmental expenditure limit (PDEL) that will ring-fence spending on projects where initial costs are offset by future savings. Starting with the next spending review, eligible preventative initiatives—such as rough sleeping programmes and early-years support—cannot be raided for immediate needs. The Institute for Government notes this could either transform government by injecting long-termism into public spending, or trigger disputes over what qualifies as preventative. The policy applies a blanket approach across all departments, unlike other nations that protect only specific sectors like public health; nearly any spending could theoretically be argued preventative, making eligibility determination a significant challenge.

headline: Ministers Extend Palantir NHS Contract to 2029 Instead of Ending It
summary: The Department of Health and Social Care has extended the controversial US tech firm Palantir's contract to provide the NHS's federated data platform—the software that links different healthcare providers—by two more years, to 2029, rather than exercising a break clause available next spring. The extension is intended to allow time to identify and line up British companies to replace Palantir when the contract ends.

headline: Nearly One Million Young People Now NEET as Government Eyes Milburn Plan
summary: Almost a million young people—one in eight—in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEET), reaching the highest level in a decade. Alan Milburn's landmark review, published today, proposes a comprehensive overhaul to address the crisis. The report recommends a legal guarantee of a route into education, training or work for every young person; a new Youth Opportunity Service; doubling apprenticeship numbers; faster mental health support without waiting for diagnosis; and gradually cutting national insurance paid by employers on workers aged under 25. Milburn estimates the plan would result in roughly 440,000 more young people in sustained work by 2036, and aims to reduce the NEET rate from about 13% to 5%, making the UK one of Europe's best performers on youth participation. The underlying issue is partly demographic: without major intervention, over a million young people could be out of work or education by 2031.

headline: Britain explores closer EU ties as post-Brexit trade-offs loom
summary: Britain is seeking to strengthen its relationship with the European Union, but efforts to rebuild ties are bringing trade-off discussions back to the fore. The story reflects the ongoing tensions between deepening EU cooperation and the commitments made during the Brexit referendum.

headline: IMF nears $1.6 billion aid deal with Ukraine pending financing assurances
summary: The International Monetary Fund says it is close to finalizing a $1.6 billion financial package for Ukraine, contingent on securing additional financing commitments from other sources. The agreement would provide crucial economic support as Ukraine continues navigating the impacts of Russia's ongoing invasion.

headline: Russian strikes damage critical infrastructure in Kyiv, disrupting water and power
summary: Russian missile strikes hit two bridges in Kyiv, Ukraine's capital, causing widespread water and power outages according to the city's mayor. The attacks represent a continued pattern of Russian targeting of civilian infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.

headline: Five EU countries begin talks with Rwanda on migrant deportation hub
summary: Austria announced that five European Union countries are initiating negotiations with Rwanda to establish a deportation hub, part of broader EU efforts to manage migration flows. The initiative reflects some EU member states' push for external migration processing arrangements outside European territory.
